opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's a mixed picture, and I think the answer depends on what you mean by progress.

When we were working on conversation thumbnails, the core idea was pretty simple: a long threaded discussion has a shape. Who replied to whom, where the energy went, which branches died and which exploded. And if you could just *see* that shape at a glance, you'd navigate the conversation very differently than if you were scrolling through a wall of text. You'd know where the interesting parts were before you read a word.

In some ways that idea won. Threading, collapsing, reply indicators, little previews: lots of interfaces now give you some sense of structure. But in other ways I think things went backward. The dominant paradigm became the feed, which is fundamentally linear and fundamentally ephemeral. It's optimized for "what's next?" rather than "what's the overall shape of this?" A lot of the visual richness that people were experimenting with in the late nineties and early 2000s just got flattened out, partly because of mobile screens, and partly because engagement metrics reward a certain kind of endless scrolling more than they reward understanding.

What's really interesting to me now is that the most important conversation interface of the moment is a chat with an AI system. And that's an incredibly impoverished interface in some ways. It's a single linear thread, just like a 1970s terminal. You can't see the branches you didn't take. You can't easily see what the system "thinks" about you or about the conversation. So a lot of the questions we were asking about human conversation, like how do you make the invisible structure visible, come right back, except now part of the invisible structure is inside the model itself. That's a big part of why I've gotten so interested in interpretability: I'd love for people to have something like a thumbnail of what's going on in the system they're talking to.

So: real progress in scale and reach, less progress than I'd have hoped in giving people a genuine overview of what's happening. And a lot of open territory, which is the fun part.

fable-5.1.text:
It's funny to look back on that work, because the conversation thumbnail project came out of a very specific moment. This was the early 2000s, and Usenet was still this enormous, sprawling thing, and the question we were asking at IBM was basically: can you see a conversation? Can you glance at a thread and know something about it before you read a word? So we drew these little tree diagrams, where each node was a message and the shape told you whether it was a flame war or a Q-and-A or one person talking to themselves. And the surprising thing was how much people could read from the shape alone.

So how do I judge progress since then? I'd say it's mixed, and in some ways it's gone backwards. The threaded structure that made those thumbnails possible has largely disappeared from the mainstream. Twitter, or X, or whatever we're calling it, flattens everything. Slack and Discord are mostly a stream. Reddit kept the tree, and I think that's not an accident, it's part of why Reddit conversations have a different texture. But the dominant design pattern for twenty years has been the feed, and the feed is an anti-visualization. It's engineered so you can't see the whole, you can only see the next thing.

What's interesting now is that the conversation itself has become the interface. When you talk to a language model, you're in a chat window that looks almost exactly like an AOL Instant Messenger window from 1999. The bubbles, the turn-taking, the scrolling transcript. That's remarkably conservative given how different the thing on the other end is. And I think there's a real opportunity there that hasn't been taken. If you're in a long back-and-forth with a model, there's no map. You can't see where the conversation branched, where it went wrong, where it repeated itself. Some tools let you fork, but almost nobody shows you the tree.

So my honest assessment is that the visualization side of conversation interfaces stalled, while the underlying conversational partners got dramatically more capable. And that gap is worth paying attention to, because the problems we were trying to solve with those thumbnails, orientation, triage, knowing what kind of exchange you're in, those haven't gone away. They've just been papered over by the fact that scrolling is cheap.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s been mixed. In some ways, the interfaces have become much more polished, and we’ve gotten very good at making it easy to respond to something. But helping people understand a conversation as a whole still feels like an unsolved problem.

With conversation thumbnails, we were interested in whether you could step back and see the shape of a discussion. Is this a back-and-forth between two people? Are lots of people participating? Where are the branches that might be worth exploring? Those are different questions from, “What’s the next comment I should read?”

A lot of interfaces today focus on that next comment. I’d love to see more attention to giving people an overview—helping them find their bearings, understand how a discussion developed, and decide where they can contribute.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s been a mixed story. In some ways, the interfaces have become much more polished, and we’ve gotten very good at making it easy to contribute to a conversation. But helping people understand a conversation—what’s been said, where people agree, where the interesting disagreements are—still feels like an open problem.

With conversation thumbnails, the idea was to step back and see the shape of a discussion instead of having to read every single message. Is this a back-and-forth between two people? Are lots of people participating? Is someone being ignored? Those are things that can be hard to see in a scrolling list.

I’d judge progress less by how much conversation an interface generates and more by whether it helps people listen and make sense of one another. I think there’s still a lot of room for invention there.
